hypotheses.justification: First countability of X is only used because the proof applies continuousAt_of_dominated, which needs 𝓝 x₀ to be countably generated. The theorem is true without it, by a direct epsilon argument. Fix x₀ and ε>0. By continuity of f.uncurry and compactness of s (tube lemma), there is a neighbourhood V of x₀ with ‖f x y − f x₀ y‖ < ε for all x ∈ V and y ∈ s. Each f x is continuous, so it is bounded on s and, via SecondCountableTopologyEither Y E, AE-strongly measurable, hence integrable on s because μ s < ∞ (s compact, μ locally finite). The set {y | ‖f x y − f x₀ y‖ ≤ ε} is closed, hence measurable by OpensMeasurableSpace Y, and contains s, so the bound holds μ.restrict s-a.e. Hence ‖∫_s f x − ∫_s f x₀‖ ≤ ε·μ(s).toReal for x ∈ V, which gives continuity at x₀. Nothing degenerates when s is empty or has measure zero. The two removable hypotheses (this one and LocallyCompactSpace X) can each be removed alone and also both together.

Local compactness of X is only used to get a compact neighbourhood U of x₀, which supplies the uniform bound M. The tube-lemma argument gives a neighbourhood V of x₀ on which sup over y∈s of ‖f x y − f x₀ y‖ < ε, using only compactness of s and continuity of f.uncurry. No local compactness of X is needed for this. The ε·μ(s) estimate then yields continuity at x₀ exactly as described for FirstCountableTopology X. Measurability and integrability come from SecondCountableTopologyEither Y E, IsLocallyFiniteMeasure μ, hs and OpensMeasurableSpace Y, which stay. The statement is therefore true without it. It can be removed on its own and also together with FirstCountableTopology X.
